component.name: TuxShell
component.summary: Manage and connect to your SSH hosts

description.p: TuxShell keeps your SSH hosts in one place and connects with the system ssh, so your ~/.ssh/config, keys, agents and jump hosts work as they already do.

ul.li: Saved hosts with groups, tags, jump hosts and an optional operating system logo
Import from ~/.ssh/config, CSV, Excel, MobaXterm, Remmina, PuTTY and Ansible inventories
Tabs and split view with up to four panes, and typing broadcast to several panes
A file browser that reuses the open SSH connection
Snippets, local port forwards and SOCKS tunnels
Remote desktops (RDP) in their own window or inside a tab
Passwords from 1Password references or the system keyring, and the 1Password SSH agent

description.p: TuxShell is free and open source. Apart from your own connections, its only network request is an optional check for a newer version at startup (on by default, off in Preferences → About; the Flathub version leaves updates to Flathub). It never downloads or installs anything itself.

screenshot.caption: Split view with the open tabs and hosts in the left panel
Home with your hosts, grouped and with live status
File panel next to a terminal

description.p: Saved layouts reopen a set of tabs and split panes in one go. Remote desktops can share printers, smart cards and USB devices or open a single program, and Windows .rdp files can be imported. Also: host groups you can create and rename, a resizable hosts sidebar, window start options, an OS Detect button, Proxmox logos and copy on select by default.

Make, rename and delete host groups from the sidebar. On macOS, TuxShell starts again (1.4.1 and 1.4.2 opened an empty window) and shows its own icon. The .flatpak from GitHub checks for updates again.

Ready for Flathub: in the Flatpak, local shell tabs, the 1Password CLI and FreeRDP run on your system, and updates come from Flathub. Preferences shows where your settings and recordings are really kept.

Change, turn off or reset any shortcut in Preferences, tabs close by themselves when you log out, clicking a host on Home no longer opens the editor (right-click does), and Remmina imports bring their passwords along.
TuxShell now also runs on macOS (beta). On Linux, Preferences shows the real settings and recordings folders.
Sign in with passwords from 1Password (op:// references, never stored), optionally use the 1Password SSH agent, and hide the ~/.ssh/config import reminder on Home.
Faster: typing, switching tabs and resizing the window no longer lag while a terminal prints a lot, and changing a setting no longer redraws every terminal.

Remote desktops (RDP), in their own window or inside a TuxShell tab, with shared folders, copy and paste, and file transfer. Open tabs can live in the left panel, and host groups and hosts can be reordered by dragging.
Connection history with search and reconnect, and session recording (screen output only) with a built-in player.
The file panel can rename, delete, create folders, change permissions, edit files in your desktop editor and follow the terminal's folder.
Terminal profiles per host: custom colours, background images, pane header colours, scrolling and bell options, and a command to run on connect.
Optional saved passwords, kept only in the system keyring and off by default. A password box appears when a server asks for a password.
The import window no longer opens empty on some systems. GNOME Software and App Center show TuxShell's icon, description and license.
Import hosts from CSV, Excel, MobaXterm, Remmina, PuTTY and Ansible, with a preview and a CSV template. Export as JSON, CSV or ssh_config. Optional operating system logos.
About page and an optional check for updates. The dock shows the TuxShell icon.
New app icon. Files on Home opens this computer.
New design with a Home page, host status, snippets and tunnels.
First release.
